title: Basic Vehicle Control
summary: How to sit, shift, brake and turn a motorcycle the way the MSF manual teaches.

blocks.text: A good riding position lets you reach every control, steer well and react quickly to hazards.

rows: Sit far enough forward that your arms are slightly bent when you hold the handgrips. Bent arms let you press on the handlebars without reaching.
Hold the grips firmly so you keep control over rough surfaces. Start with your right wrist flat so you do not accidentally give it too much throttle.
Adjust them so your hands are even with or below your elbows. This lets you use the right muscles to steer.
Keep them against the gas tank to help you balance as the motorcycle turns.
Keep them firmly on the footrests and near the controls. Do not drag your feet.

blocks.text: Do not let your toes point downward. They can get caught between the road and the footrests.

items: The gearshift lever is in front of the left footrest and is worked by your left foot.
Shift up: put your foot under the lever, lift and release.
Shift down: press the lever down and release.
Each lift or press changes one gear. A spring returns the lever to center after each shift.
A typical pattern is 1-N-2-3-4-5. Neutral sits between 1st and 2nd: a half lift from 1st or a half press from 2nd.
Most motorcycles have five gears, but some have four or six.

blocks.text: Shift up well before the engine reaches its maximum recommended RPM. Shift soon enough to avoid over-revving, but not so soon that the engine lugs.

items: Roll off the throttle as you squeeze the clutch lever.
Lift the shift lever firmly as far as it will go, then release.
Smoothly ease out the clutch lever and adjust the throttle.

blocks.text: Downshift as you slow or stop, or when you need more power to accelerate. Downshift in three steps:

items: Roll off the throttle as you squeeze the clutch lever.
Press the shift lever down firmly and release.
Ease out the clutch lever as you roll on the throttle slightly. This helps the engine come up to speed and makes the shift smoother.

blocks.text: Be sure you are going slowly enough before you shift into a lower gear. If not, the motorcycle will lurch and the rear wheel may skid. Going downhill or shifting into first, you may need to brake first to slow down enough.

Engine braking is the slowing effect you get when you shift to a lower gear. To use it smoothly, shift down one gear at a time and ease the clutch out through the friction zone between shifts, staying there until engine speed settles.

items: Stay in first gear while you are stopped, so you can move out quickly if you need to.
Change gears before you enter a turn. If you must shift in a turn, do it smoothly: a sudden change in power to the rear wheel can cause a skid.

blocks.text: Improper braking is a significant factor in many motorcycle crashes. Most motorcycles have two brake controls: a front brake lever on the right handgrip and a rear brake pedal under your right foot. Use both brakes every time you slow or stop. Doing it on normal stops builds the habit you need in an emergency.

The front brake is the more powerful one. It can supply 70% or more of your total stopping power, and it is safe to use when you use it properly. Maximum straight-line braking means fully applying both brakes without locking either wheel:

items: Squeeze the front brake smoothly and firmly, with gradually more force. Never grab the lever or use sudden pressure.
As the bike's weight shifts forward, the front tire gets more traction, so you can apply the front brake more firmly.
Keep your knees against the tank and your eyes up, looking well ahead, so you stop in a straight line.
Use light-to-lighter pressure on the rear pedal. With weight moving forward, the rear wheel has less traction and can skid.

blocks.text: Grabbing the front brake or stomping on the rear pedal can lock a wheel and cause loss of control.
Any lean reduces the traction available for braking. The more you lean, the more likely the tires are to lose grip.

items: If road and traffic conditions allow, straighten the motorcycle so it is as upright as possible, then brake.
If you cannot straighten first, brake smoothly and gradually, using less force than you would when upright.
As you slow and the lean decreases, you can brake more firmly.
By the time you stop, the motorcycle should be upright with the handlebars squared.

rows: Front and rear brakes are connected. Using either the lever or the pedal applies pressure to both.
A type of linked system. Pressing the rear brake also applies some front braking.
Prevents wheels from locking and skidding in a panic stop. Sensors release and reapply pressure, more than 15 times per second.

blocks.text: Systems differ between models. Check your owner's manual to learn how yours works.

Riders often take curves too fast. When they cannot hold the turn, they drift into another lane or off the road, or they panic and brake too hard and skid. These four steps help (in real riding they may overlap):

items: SLOW: reduce speed before the turn by closing the throttle and, if needed, using both brakes.
LOOK: look through the turn to where you want to go. Turn just your head, not your shoulders, and keep your eyes level with the horizon.
PRESS: to turn, a motorcycle must lean. Press the handgrip on the side you want to go: press left, lean left, go left. Press right, lean right, go right.
ROLL: roll on the throttle to keep or slightly increase speed. This steadies the motorcycle.

blocks.caption: A curve ahead: slow down before you enter it, not in the middle of it.

items: The faster you go or the sharper the turn, the more you need to lean.
Normal turns: you and the motorcycle lean together at the same angle.
Slow, tight turns (like a parking-lot U-turn): lean only the motorcycle and keep your body upright.
Pressing the grip to start a lean is called countersteering. Conventional three-wheel motorcycles cannot lean, so they cannot countersteer; the rider points the front wheel where they want to go.

keyPoints: Sit with arms slightly bent, right wrist flat, hands at or below elbows, knees on the tank and feet on the footrests.
The left foot shifts: lift to go up, press to go down; neutral is a half lift from 1st or half press from 2nd.
Slow down enough before downshifting or the rear wheel may skid; stay in first gear while stopped.
Shift before a turn, not in it; if you must, shift smoothly.
Use both brakes every time; the front brake gives 70% or more of your stopping power.
Squeeze the front brake progressively and use light-to-lighter rear pressure; never grab or stomp.
In a curve, straighten up before braking if you can; otherwise brake gently.
Turn with SLOW, LOOK, PRESS, ROLL: press the grip on the side you want to go.
